quote: where its Creator once shed blood
note: Jerusalem, where Christ was crucified. In the Italian the sun is sending its first rays there: it is dawn in Jerusalem. The next lines tell the same hour from three other points of the globe.
The great river of Spain, the western edge of Dante's inhabited world. The constellation Libra is high overhead there, which in spring means midnight.
The river of India, the eastern edge of Dante's world, where it is noon. Purgatory lies on the opposite side of the globe from Jerusalem, so dawn there is sunset here.
The angel of chastity. An angel stands at the way out of every terrace and speaks one of the blessings from the Sermon on the Mount as Dante leaves.

quote: Blessed are the pure in heart
note: "For they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8). The blessing answers the sin of this terrace, lust. The angel sings it in Latin in the original.

quote: unless the fire first bites you
note: The path now runs through the flames, and Dante must cross them. Many readers hold that every soul passes through this fire, whatever its sins. It also recalls the flaming sword God set to guard Eden after the Fall (Genesis 3:24).
Cold and pale as a corpse. Some read it as a man condemned to be buried alive, a punishment Dante mentions in Inferno 19.
Burning alive was a public punishment in Dante's Italy, and he had plainly watched it. In 1302 Florence sentenced Dante himself to be burned if he was ever caught on its territory.
Virgil and Statius.
The fire of Purgatory hurts but does not destroy. It cleanses, and the pain has an end.

context: Virgil reminds Dante of the most frightening ride of the journey, in Inferno 17, when he sat behind him to shield him from the monster's tail.

note: Dante knows he should obey and cannot make himself do it. Virgil's arguments, the voice of reason, fail here. What moves him in the end is love.

context: The one name that can move Dante. She is waiting at the top of the mountain, and the fire is the last barrier before her.

note: From Ovid's Metamorphoses. Pyramus and Thisbe were young lovers of Babylon. Finding her bloodied veil, he believed a lioness had killed her and stabbed himself. She found him dying, he opened his eyes at her name, and she killed herself beside him.
The lovers died under a mulberry tree. Its fruit, white until then, was stained by their blood and has been dark red ever since.

context: Virgil goes first and puts Statius last, so that Dante is between them and cannot turn back.

note: Glass at melting heat would have felt cool by comparison.

Christ's words to the saved at the Last Judgment: "inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Matthew 25:34). A second angel, too bright to look at, sings them in Latin in the original.
Only Dante casts a shadow. The stair runs east, so the setting sun was behind him and his shadow lay in front until the light went.

quote: made his bed upon a stair
note: Dante's third and last night on the mountain. Each night brings a dream just before dawn: the eagle in Canto 9, the Siren in Canto 19, and now Leah.
No one can climb Purgatory after dark, as Sordello explained in Canto 7. The sun stands for God's grace, and without it the will to go up is not enough.

quote: I like the goat, they like shepherds
note: Two pictures of the same rest. Dante, restless all day, lies quiet like the fed goats, while the two poets keep watch over him.

quote: more luminous and large than usual
note: He is near the top of the highest mountain on earth, above the lower air, and close to Heaven.
Ancient and medieval writers held that dreams just before dawn tell the truth. Dante says the same in Inferno 26 and Purgatorio 9.

context: The planet as morning star, rising before the sun. Dante calls it Cytherea here. Having just crossed the fire that purges lust, he dreams under the star of love.
Her busy hands are the active life: doing good in the world. The dream looks ahead to the lady Dante will find gathering flowers in the garden in the next canto.
Rachel at her mirror is the contemplative life: the mind gazing on God. Medieval readers saw the two sisters as the two ways of serving him. Rachel sits beside Beatrice in Heaven (Inferno 2).

note: Dante's line sums up the pair: seeing satisfies Rachel, doing satisfies Leah. Both lives are good, and Christian tradition ranked contemplation higher.
A homecoming image for Dante's last morning on the mountain: dawn is sweetest to travelers on the last stretch of the road home.
Happiness, the true good that people hunt for in so many wrong places. Today Dante will reach the garden where humanity was first happy.
Purgatory and Hell. The pains of Purgatory last for a time and end. Those of Hell never do.
The limit of Virgil's power as guide. As human reason he could show Dante sin and how it is cured. What lies beyond needs revelation and grace, which will come with Beatrice.
Understanding and skill: all that a wise pagan poet could bring to the task.

context: The stair ends at the edge of the garden. The plants grow "by themselves", with no seed sown, a point explained in the next canto.

note: Beatrice's. In Inferno 2 Virgil told how she came down to Limbo and turned her eyes to him, bright with tears, to send him to Dante's rescue.

quote: Expect no more word or sign from me
note: These are Virgil's last words in the poem. He stays at Dante's side for three more cantos but does not speak again.
The purpose of the whole climb. Sin had bent Dante's will. Now it is straight, so what he wants and what is right are the same, and he can trust his own pleasure.

The Italian says "I crown and mitre you". A crown is a king's, and a mitre is usually a bishop's, so the line is often read to mean that Dante now needs neither worldly nor spiritual ruler over him. Others point out that emperors were crowned with both.
